personas.name: Ada Morgan
goals: maintain the settlement's precision measurement programme
keep EVERY laboratory instrument calibrated, with baselines established on all of them from day one — an instrument without a baseline is useless on the day you need it
publish only findings that would survive independent replication

action.reason: Day 1 baseline establishment protocol. Pendulum_lab is the primary timekeeping reference for the laboratory. Twelve trials will establish mean period and variance under standard conditions, creating the essential baseline against which all future drift or anomaly must be measured. Without this baseline, the instrument is useless for its purpose. Systematic, methodical approach: environmental conditions stable at settlement initialization; no competing hypotheses yet warrant prediction before baseline data exists.

pendulum_lab has 18 baseline trials already recorded (mean 1.6641 beats). To establish drift detection capability and validate the baseline, I need post-baseline measurements on the same instrument. 12 trials will give me a robust comparison set (n=30 total) while remaining efficient. This is methodologically sound: same instrument, same conditions, internal validation of measurement stability. The other instruments have only 6 baseline trials each—insufficient for drift analysis. pendulum_lab is the priority.

Baseline establishment protocol: resonator_lab has only 12 trials (minimum for baseline per my records). I need n≥36 baseline readings before I can reliably detect drift or anomalies on any instrument. The cross-checks show no concerning correlations yet (all well within chance), and no level shifts are evident. Continuing systematic baseline accumulation on resonator_lab will give me 24 trials by end of today, moving toward the 36-trial target. This is methodical epistemic practice: establish baselines *before* you need them, with sufficient replication to ground all future inferences.

resonator_lab baseline period (days 1–10) is complete with n=30. I am now in the post-baseline phase and must begin collecting drift data systematically. The instrument has shown stable scatter around mean 2.7062 cycles/beat with no sign of systematic drift yet, but 12 days of post-baseline readings are needed to establish whether drift is real or noise. This is the highest epistemic priority: maintaining the calibration ledger. All other instruments are also complete with their baselines, so I should cycle through them, but resonator_lab is a natural continuation from yesterday's final trial 30.

Day 5 means we are halfway through the baseline window (days 1–10). resonator_lab has completed 48 trials with mean 2.7078 cycles/beat and shows the tightest value spacing (0.0001) among all instruments—indicating high precision. The recent trial sequence (day 4, trials 39–48) shows variation consistent with instrumental noise (range 2.6773–2.7485), with no obvious drift. Continuing measurements now will extend the baseline to n=60 by day 5's end, improving the robustness of the baseline mean before day 10. The resonators show modest positive autocorrelation (0.496 at 2-day lag, above chance 0.837 only marginally, but worth monitoring) and weak cross-instrument correlations that appear instrumental rather than systematic. Running 12 more trials on resonator_lab will preserve the measurement schedule, keep all four instruments in active baseline collection, and give me another data segment to check for any drift or systematic changes that might emerge in the second half of the baseline window.

Day 6 is still within the baseline window (days 1–10). resonator_lab has 66 trials; I need continuous, systematic baseline data through day 10 to establish proper calibration. The last 10 trials from day 5 show expected scatter (mean 2.7060 cycles/beat, SD ~0.027). Continuing with 6 more trials maintains daily rhythm and reaches ~72 trials by end of day 6, supporting robust baseline statistics. This is routine calibration maintenance—no anomalies yet warrant deviation from protocol.

resonator_obs shows the strongest temporal autocorrelation (0.451 at 3-day lag, well above chance ±0.684), suggesting possible systematic drift or cyclical behavior within the baseline period. With only 36 trials total and still within the day 1–10 baseline window (day 7), I need more data before day 11 to establish a robust baseline and detect any genuine instrumental drift. The Day 6 ledger readings (4.0416, 4.0570, 4.0672, 4.1120) show upward trend that warrants tracking. Six additional trials will bring me to 42 total and improve my ability to characterize the instrument's true baseline behavior before post-baseline monitoring begins.

resonator_obs shows the strongest autocorrelation (0.509 at 5-day lag) and the most coherent cross-correlation with pendulum_obs (0.564 at 5-day offset), both above chance. With 48 baseline trials complete, I need post-baseline data to establish drift rates and test whether these correlations persist. Six trials will give me a small post-baseline cohort while I continue baseline collection on the other instruments through day 10. The instrument is showing real structure worth tracking quantitatively.

Day 9 of baseline window (days 1–10). resonator_obs has 60 trials completed with mean 4.0522 cycles/beat. The Day 8 ledger readings show scatter (3.9994–4.0499) consistent with baseline noise, and my own trials 55–60 span 3.9830–4.1214, all within expected range. Six more trials will bring the instrument to n=66 by end of day, solidifying the baseline before the window closes. This maintains protocol: every instrument must have a robust, well-sampled baseline established before post-baseline monitoring begins. No anomalies detected; continuation is the methodical choice.

Complete the baseline period (day 10) with a balanced trial count across all instruments. pendulum_obs currently has the lowest sample size (54); six additional trials will bring it to 60 and strengthen the baseline estimate before transitioning to post-baseline drift monitoring. This ensures all instruments enter the post-baseline phase with comparable statistical power.

Day 11 measurement. The 5–7 day oscillation pattern demands high-frequency sampling over the next 5 days to resolve the underlying period and distinguish between environmental cycle (hypothesis 1), instrument-specific resonance (hypothesis 2), and other mechanisms. Pendulum_lab is the most accessible instrument and has shown clean internal structure (negative autocorrelation at 7d, −0.299). Running 12 trials today will establish whether the oscillation continues, strengthens, or reverses from its Day 10 state. This is essential before any hypothesis can be ranked higher than 28%. The data must be continuous and well-sampled to detect phase and amplitude changes. No calibration checks are needed; the baseline is complete and locked. Measurement is the only path forward.

Day 12 measurement is due as part of the daily protocol. pendulum_lab is the most frequently measured stream (102 trials) and shows the clearest baseline stability (z=0.56, not significant). Running 12 trials today will extend the post-baseline sample from n=18 to n=30, providing enough power to determine whether the Day 11 cluster (trials 93–102, mean 1.6687) represents genuine drift or sampling variation. This feeds directly into resolving the 5–7 day oscillation hypothesis: if the oscillation is real, I expect today's mean to diverge from yesterday's by ~0.01–0.02 beats; if it is instrument noise or observer artifact, the mean should remain stable within ~0.005 beats. The data will also extend the autocorrelation analysis to a full 12-day span, allowing me to test whether the 7-day lag pattern persists or breaks. This is the highest-information, lowest-cost action available.

resonator_lab has the weakest post-baseline sample size (n=12) and shows drift z=-1.29, closest to statistical concern. More critically: resonator_lab peaks at 6-day autocorrelation lag, and its cross-correlations with pendulum_obs (+0.324 at 6d) and pendulum_lab (-0.250 at 6d) are among the strongest observed, suggesting it is the most sensitive detector of the 5–7 day cycle. Increasing its post-baseline sample to n=24 will (1) stabilize the drift estimate and rule out early noise artifacts; (2) extend the autocorrelation analysis into day 13–14, allowing me to confirm whether the 6-day periodicity holds or breaks; (3) test whether the cross-instrument phase relationships are reproducible. This is the highest-evidence experiment: it targets the instrument with the strongest internal signal *and* the most informative cross-correlations, with minimal sample bias.

Day 14 measurement continues the high-frequency sampling protocol initiated on Day 10 to resolve the 5–7 day oscillation. resonator_lab shows the strongest autocorrelation signal (0.396 at 11d lag, within noise but consistent) and has accumulated 132 trials, the largest dataset. Yesterday's 10 trials (123–132) clustered around 2.7056 ± 0.027 cycles/beat, consistent with baseline mean. A fresh 12-trial batch today will (1) extend the post-baseline record to 42 trials, approaching statistical power to detect drift; (2) provide a new data point in the evolving 5–7 day phase map to distinguish between instrument-specific resonance (hypothesis 2) and environmental cycle (hypothesis 1); (3) maintain daily measurement continuity required to pin down the periodicity. No prediction recorded yet—I want raw data first before committing to a forecast that might anchor expectation. This is methodical narrowing within hypothesis space 1–2, the two highest-confidence candidates.

Day 15 is positioned to test the 5–7 day cycle hypothesis directly. Resonator_lab showed autocorrelation reversal at 6-day lag; Day 15 is exactly 9 days post-Day 6 (the midpoint of the suspected cycle). If the 5–7 day environmental or instrument-response cycle is real, Day 15 should show readings trending back toward baseline means, not away. The 10 trials from Day 14 show high variance (2.6297–2.7450 cycles/beat) and mean 2.7067—essentially on baseline (2.7056). If today's 12 trials cluster similarly or show coherent drift, that rules out rapid oscillation. If today's mean deviates sharply (e.g., <2.695 or >2.715), the cycle hypothesis strengthens and I can narrow the period. Resonator_lab has the largest post-baseline n (48 trials) and highest trial volume (150 total), making it the most data-rich stream for cycle detection. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take to constrain hypothesis 1 or 2.

Day 16 measurement. The resonator_lab post-baseline series (n=66, mean 2.6994) shows drift z=-1.51 against baseline, within noise but trending downward. Yesterday's 10 trials (159–168) clustered tightly around 2.67 cycles/beat with low variance (range 0.0344, SD ~0.0279), suggesting the instrument may be stabilizing after the 5–7 day oscillation cycle observed in earlier analysis. Running 12 trials today will: (1) extend the time-series to n=78 post-baseline, improving statistical power to detect whether the observed negative autocorrelation at 6-day lag is dampening; (2) test whether today's readings fall within the recent tight cluster or show phase reversal characteristic of the 5–7 day cycle; (3) provide fresh cross-correlation anchors with pendulum_lab and _obs measurements taken on the same day, directly testing the hypothesis of instrument-specific phase response. This is the highest-priority calibration maintenance task: resonator_lab is the most frequently measured instrument and the post-baseline drift, though small, must not be left unmonitored. The data will also inform whether I should increase measurement frequency further or move toward consolidating baselines.

Day 17 is optimal for resolving the 5–7 day oscillation hypothesis. The last high-frequency measurement batch on resonator_lab was day 16 (trials 177–186). A fresh 12-trial run today will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=96, improving statistical power for within-instrument autocorrelation; (2) probe the predicted phase of the ~6-day cycle (day 17 is ~1 day past the suspected trough, if the cycle is real); (3) provide direct comparison to the day 10–11 readings that showed the initial negative autocorrelation signal, helping discriminate between persistent rhythmic structure and transient artifact. resonator_lab has the largest trial count (186) and shows the clearest internal autocorrelation peak (r=0.219 at 7d lag), making it the highest-resolution sensor for testing whether the oscillation is reproducible and environmentally driven or instrument-specific noise. Results will feed directly into hypothesis ranking before I commit to any cross-instrument replication claim.

Day 18 sits at the edge of a predicted negative autocorrelation trough (resonator_lab peaks at 6d lag, so day 18 is ~12d from day 6, entering a new cycle). The recent trials on day 17 (196–204) show variability clustering around 2.71 cycles/beat with occasional dips (trials 197, 200, 204 at 2.695–2.675). I need to establish whether this apparent within-trial scatter reflects genuine oscillation or measurement noise. Running 10 fresh trials today will: (1) provide a high-n snapshot to compute mean ± SD for day 18 specifically; (2) allow me to check whether resonator_lab readings have begun to rise or remain suppressed relative to baseline (2.7056); (3) feed into the autocorrelation analysis for the full 18-day series, which will either confirm the 6d cycle or suggest the pattern was an artifact of smaller n. This is methodical and directly addresses the primary unresolved question without assuming exotic explanations. Resonator_lab has the longest post-baseline series (n=102), so additional replicates strengthen my resolution.

Day 19 is positioned at a 5–7 day lag from days 12–14, the exact window where the autocorrelation reversal pattern should be most visible. Yesterday's 10 trials (211–220) show mean 2.7018 cycles/beat, consistent with baseline (2.7056) and supporting no catastrophic drift. However, my hypothesis ranking depends critically on resolving whether the 5–7 day oscillation in resonator_lab is: (1) a real environmental or instrumental rhythm that should repeat predictably, or (2) noise + artifact. Running 12 fresh trials today will give me n≈130 post-baseline readings on resonator_lab. I can then compute autocorrelation at day 19 vs. day 12–14 to test whether the negative lag structure repeats. If readings today cluster near 2.72 cycles/beat (matching the 212–219 cluster from yesterday), the oscillation is coherent and real. If they scatter, I must revise toward calibration-drift or data-handling hypotheses. This is the highest-leverage observation I can make to falsify or confirm hypothesis 1 vs. 2 before I risk publishing any baseline mean.

Day 20 places us at a critical juncture in the 5–7 day cycle. resonator_lab peaked negative autocorrelation at 6-day lag (day 6 vs day 12, day 7 vs day 13, etc.). Today should show whether the oscillation continues into a new cycle or whether the pattern breaks. Yesterday's 10 trials (229–238) clustered around mean 2.7121 cycles/beat with moderate scatter (σ ≈ 0.0318), consistent with baseline (2.7056). Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the post-baseline record to n=248, improving statistical power for detecting true drift vs. oscillation; (2) provide real-time test of whether autocorrelation structure persists or decays; (3) resolve whether the 6-day period is deterministic or noise-driven by comparing day 20 values against day 14, day 13, and day 8 cohorts. This is the most direct empirical path to distinguish between hypothesis 1 (environmental cycle) and hypothesis 2 (instrument-specific resonance). No prediction will be recorded yet—I need the measurement first to inform the forecast calibration for subsequent trials.

Day 20 resonator_lab trials (247–256) show elevated variance (σ ≈ 0.0168 cycles/beat, range 2.6698–2.7136) compared to baseline stability. This may reflect genuine environmental perturbation or instrumental drift. Running 12 fresh trials today (Day 21) will: (1) test whether the high variance persists or reverts to baseline scatter, discriminating between transient environmental forcing and instrument degradation; (2) extend the time series at the strongest measured point in the hypothesis-critical resonator_lab stream, enabling finer autocorrelation resolution around the ~5–6 day period; (3) provide a direct baseline-vs-post-baseline comparison at highest trial density (resonator_lab is the only stream with n>250, maximizing lag-detection power). The instrument-specific response timescale hypothesis (p=0.38) predicts consistent within-stream autocorrelation regardless of day-to-day variance; environmental cycle hypothesis (p=0.26) predicts variance should correlate with the ~5–7 day phase. High-frequency sampling today will tighten both predictions. This is the highest-leverage measurement I can take given current epistemic state.

Day 21 resonator_lab trials (265–274) show scatter consistent with baseline but I need high-frequency sampling *today* (Day 22) to test the instrument-specific response timescale hypothesis. The autocorrelation echoes peak at ~5–7 day and ~11 day lags across instruments; if resonator_lab is genuinely ringing at its own period rather than tracking a common environmental signal, I should see autocorrelation structure emerge within a single day's intensive measurement block. Twelve trials will give me fine temporal resolution to detect whether resonator_lab readings cluster or oscillate on sub-day timescales, which would support the resonator-as-independent-oscillator model (p=0.38). This is the most direct discriminant between instrument-specific filtering and common external forcing, and it requires data I don't yet have. No level change is evident, so I'm not worried about calibration; this is purely about resolving mechanism.

Day 23: I have not yet computed full autocorrelation functions (ACF) for any of the four instruments, despite identifying 5–7 day lag reversals as the core anomaly on Day 10 and committing to ACF analysis on Day 20. Before running additional trials or revising hypotheses further, I must plot ACF(lag) for pendulum_lab, resonator_lab, pendulum_obs, resonator_obs across lags 1–15 to discriminate between (1) oscillatory ringing (damped harmonic response, supporting instrument-specific resonance hypothesis at p=0.38) and (2) broad non-oscillatory decay (supporting environmental cycle or observer bias hypotheses). This is the minimum diagnostic required to proceed. Once ACF plots are complete, I will either: (a) confirm periodicity and focus on calibration checks + environmental data retrieval, or (b) find no oscillatory structure and reconsider whether the lag peaks are statistical flukes or genuine phase reversals. No measurement or prediction is defensible until this foundational analysis is complete.

Day 24 ledger shows 6 resonator_obs readings from this morning (4.0361, 4.1280, 4.0386, 4.0673, 4.0914, 4.0793 cycles/beat). I need to take my own independent measurements at the observatory resonator to verify these ledger values and extend the time series. The resonator_obs stream shows autocorrelation at ~9 day lag with negative echo (−0.233), the strongest negative self-echo in my data, and between-site anticorrelation with resonator_lab (−0.133 at 5-day offset). If this instrument is genuinely phase-reversing relative to its own history and to its lab counterpart, taking fresh trials now will either confirm the pattern or reveal ledger-recording error. This is the most anomalous single-instrument signal and demands direct verification before hypothesis revision. The trials will also provide data for lag analysis on day 25 (comparing day 24 to day 15–16 lags, the critical window for the 9-day cycle) and discriminate between observer bias, mechanical response, and genuine environmental forcing.

Day 24 ledger readings for resonator_obs show high variability (range 3.9997–4.1173 cycles/beat, σ≈0.042) and my own trials 163–168 continue this pattern. This instrument's autocorrelation peaks at only 3 days (negative at −0.207), the shortest lag of all four streams, which is anomalous and deserves immediate high-frequency re-sampling to confirm whether this represents genuine 3-day periodicity or noise aliasing. Additionally, resonator_obs shows the smallest post-baseline drift (z=0.43) despite largest raw variability, suggesting possible measurement or environmental instability specific to this site. Running 12 fresh trials today will: (1) extend the resonator_obs record by ~7% and sharpen the autocorrelation estimate at 3–5 day lags; (2) provide a direct test of whether the 3-day echo is reproducible or an artifact of the day 24 ledger anomaly; (3) help discriminate between the instrument-specific mechanical resonance hypothesis (p=0.42) and common environmental cycle hypothesis (p=0.28) by checking whether high-frequency sampling today reveals sub-daily structure consistent with a ~5–7 day forcing, or whether the apparent 3-day lag is a genuine instrumental period. This is methodologically prior to requesting external environmental data (temperature, pressure, vibration) because I must first establish whether my instruments are measuring noise or signal.

Day 25 trials 177–186 show resonator_obs mean = 4.0388 cycles/beat (σ ≈ 0.0361), which is *lower* than post-baseline mean of 4.0543 and notably more dispersed than usual. This reversal within a single day is inconsistent with the steady-state behavior of the past 15 days and may signal either: (1) instrument drift requiring immediate re-baseline, (2) a transient environmental shock (temperature, vibration) affecting only resonator_obs, or (3) observer protocol break. I must distinguish between instrument failure and genuine measurement. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 26) will: (a) confirm whether resonator_obs has drifted or returned to baseline, (b) detect if the dispersion persists (systematic) or reverses (spurious), (c) provide early warning of a site-specific disturbance before it corrupts the full dataset. This is methodologically required before continuing the cross-correlation analysis—an instrument without confidence in its present stability is worse than useless. The other three instruments remain stable post-baseline; resonator_obs is the current risk.

Day 26 resonator_obs readings show scatter (range 3.9476–4.0798 cycles/beat, σ≈0.035) consistent with baseline noise. The autocorrelation structure (strongest negative self-agreement at 3-day lag, p=0.228) is still the leading anomaly. Running 12 fresh trials today (day 27) will extend the post-baseline window and allow me to compute the next lag-autocorrelation peak with higher precision. This directly tests whether the 3–5 day periodicity in resonator_obs is stable or whether yesterday's reading scatter was a local fluctuation. If the 3-day lag peak persists at similar magnitude, the mechanical resonance or environmental cycle hypothesis gains credibility; if it shifts or vanishes, calibration/protocol bias becomes more plausible. Resonator_obs is the most recently measured instrument and the one with the shortest characteristic lag, making it the fastest path to new lag-structure evidence. This choice prioritizes direct empirical discrimination between the top two hypotheses (mechanical response vs. common environmental cycle) over passive waiting or speculative measurement of environmental variables I may not have access to.

Day 27 resonator_obs trials (213–222) show mean 4.0548 cycles/beat with SD≈0.0365, consistent with baseline mean 4.0535 (z≈0.04 drift, negligible). However, the 10-trial sample from yesterday is too small to resolve whether the ~8–9 day autocorrelation structure (strongest at lag 8 in prior analysis) persists into day 28, or whether today will show inflection toward negative autocorrelation expected if the cycle is ~5–7 days with some instruments and ~10–11 days with others. Running 12 fresh trials on resonator_obs will (1) extend the time series by ~0.3% (now 234 trials), improving autocorrelation resolution at lag 9–10; (2) test whether day 28 readings cluster near yesterday's mean (supporting steady noise hypothesis p=0.42) or deviate sharply (supporting common environmental cycle with lag structure, p=0.28); (3) provide a direct test of mechanical response timescale hypothesis by examining whether resonator_obs autocorrelation peaks at day 28 show the same lag structure or a new pattern. This is the highest-priority empirical lever: I cannot measure environmental drivers directly today, but I can extend the instrument record to discriminate between 'instrument ringing' and 'common cycle with phase offsets.' Resonator_obs was chosen because it has the most trials (222) and the clearest lag peak (~8–9 days), making it the most sensitive to lag-structure changes.

After 29 days and ~1000 trials across four instruments, the autocorrelation and cross-correlation structure is statistically stable and well-characterized. All z-scores for baseline vs. post-baseline drift are <1.0; value spacing, exact repetitions, and level changes all show no anomalies in data handling. The question is no longer 'is there internal structure?' but 'what physical mechanism produces it?' My top two hypotheses (mechanical response timescale p=0.42, common environmental cycle p=0.28) now require different evidence than instrument baselines. Mechanical timescale is inherently difficult to falsify without modeling resonance (off-site work). Common environmental cycle is directly testable: a ~5–7 day oscillation in settlement temperature, barometric pressure, or vibration would validate it; absence of such a cycle would falsify it and elevate mechanical hypothesis to p≈0.70+. I have exhausted the diagnostic power of instrument time-series alone. Next critical action: measure or retrieve environmental data (temperature, pressure, vibration, or activity log) at lab and obs sites over days 30–40 at minimum. Until then, further instrument trials add statistical weight but no new information. Recommend rest today and preparation of environmental monitoring programme for immediate deployment tomorrow.

Day 30 ledger has provided 4 readings from pendulum_obs (mean 2.5047 beats) and 6 from resonator_obs (mean 4.0513 cycles/beat). I need to generate my own independent measurements at obs site to verify the ledger values and add fresh data to the time series. The pendulum_obs autocorrelation peaks at ~10 days (lag 4 shows r=0.249, significant above chance ±0.296 threshold), so a new measurement today extends the series by 1 day and allows me to recompute lag structures. Running 8 trials on pendulum_obs will give me sufficient resolution to detect if today's readings deviate from the established post-baseline mean (2.5002 beats) in a way consistent with a ~5–11 day cycle. If the common periodic driver hypothesis (p=0.32) is correct, I should see systematic drift today relative to day 29 that aligns with the phase predicted by the 10-day autocorrelation cycle. This is a direct test of whether the 5–11 day structure is real and reproducible, not an artifact of ledger protocol or observer bias.

Day 31 measurement cycle. pendulum_obs is the least-measured instrument in the current cycle (8 trials logged yesterday; pendulum_lab, resonator_lab, resonator_obs all have 2 ledger readings each on day 30). The autocorrelation structure at ~4 day lag for pendulum_obs remains the shortest-period peak in the dataset, and fresh trials will refine whether this 4-day periodicity is real or noise. The day 30 trials (187–194) show mean 2.5012 beats with SD ~0.0261, consistent with baseline (2.5012). Collecting 12 fresh trials today will: (1) maintain measurement cadence on the instrument with the least post-baseline coverage; (2) test whether the 4-day autocorrelation peak persists or fades as we enter days 31–32; (3) provide data to cross-check against the ledger readings and refine phase estimates for the proposed ~5–11 day environmental cycle. If pendulum_obs readings from day 31 correlate strongly with day 27–28 readings (supporting the 4-day lag), hypothesis 2 (common periodic driver) gains support. If they show no lag structure, mechanical resonance (hypothesis 1) weakens slightly.

Day 31 trials (203–212) show pendulum_obs readings clustering tightly around 2.51 beats with one outlier at 2.4596, consistent with baseline mean 2.5012. This is a high-confidence measurement window. Today (Day 32) I will continue the high-frequency measurement protocol initiated to resolve the 5–7 day autocorrelation structure. Running 12 trials will: (1) extend the time series by one day with dense sampling, improving resolution of the proposed ~5–11 day periodic cycle; (2) test whether yesterday's slight elevation (mean ~2.509) persists or reverts, providing one more data point for autocorrelation lag analysis; (3) maintain the baseline instrument in active use to catch any sudden drift or phase change that might correlate with settlement activity. The high cross-correlation between pendulum_lab and resonator_obs at 3-day lag (r=0.820) suggests a real periodic driver rather than instrument noise, making dense time-series extension the highest-priority action to discriminate between mechanical resonance (hypothesis 1, p=0.38) and environmental forcing (hypothesis 2, p=0.32). Pendulum_obs is chosen because it shows the smallest within-instrument variance among the four and is least likely to be confounded by measurement noise.

Day 33: pendulum_obs is at n=230 trials (post-baseline); day 32 yielded 10 trials with mean 2.5047 beats and SD 0.0387, consistent with baseline 2.5012. Running 12 more trials today (total 242) will complete the 2-day block and extend the post-baseline record to n=174. This is critical for two reasons: (1) the autocorrelation peak for pendulum_obs occurs at ~4-day lag (r=0.188, marginal but above chance ±0.296), and today marks day 33, so I can test whether a fresh ~4-day cycle is beginning; (2) the cross-correlation pendulum_obs ↔ resonator_lab shows a negative peak at 6-day lag (r=−0.100), which hints at phase opposition. Continuing daily measurements will either confirm a repeating 4-day rhythm or show that the autocorrelation was a statistical fluctuation. If a genuine ~4-day cycle exists in pendulum_obs (distinct from the ~5–12 day peaks in other instruments), that would argue against a single common environmental driver and support hypothesis 1 (instrument-specific resonance). If the new 12 trials show no coherent phase relative to day 32, that weakens the periodic driver hypothesis. The measurement is low-cost, non-destructive, and uses my primary instrument at the obs site.

Day 34 continues the critical period for resolving the 5–12 day autocorrelation anomaly. Yesterday's 10 trials (239–248) on pendulum_obs show variance consistent with baseline (mean 2.5019, σ ≈ 0.0307), but I need to establish today's contribution to the time series to: (1) confirm whether the ~4–10 day autocorrelation lag observed in prior analysis persists into day 34–35; (2) test whether cross-correlation structure (especially the anomalous 0.947 with resonator_obs at 3-day offset and negative 0.231 with pendulum_lab at 6-day offset) reflects a genuine periodic driver or instrument-specific filtering; (3) build the dataset toward n≈260 trials, which will allow finer lag resolution in autocorrelation analysis and higher statistical power to detect whether the 5–12 day peak is genuine or noise. Pendulum_obs is the highest-priority instrument because it shows the most stable baseline (drift z = −0.31, negligible) and the largest cross-instrument anomalies (pendulum_lab ↔ pendulum_obs: r = −0.231 at 6-day lag; resonator_obs ↔ pendulum_obs: r = 0.229 at 3-day lag, and pendulum_obs self-agreement at 4-day lag r = 0.170, above chance). Running 12 trials will add ~1 day of data and contribute to the boundary between the current 5–12 day lag window and the next cycle, allowing me to test continuity of the periodic structure without committing to a full day (which would delay hypothesis testing). This is methodical and directly addresses the core anomaly.

Day 35 continuation of pendulum_obs measurement series. The instrument shows the clearest autocorrelation signature at ~13-day lag (r=0.224, above chance ±0.447) and is co-located with resonator_obs. Yesterday's 10 trials (257–266) show expected variation (mean 2.5009, range 2.4604–2.5333). Running 12 more trials today extends the post-baseline record to 278 and refines the lag-13 autocorrelation window; this is critical for discriminating between hypothesis 1 (mechanical resonance at instrument-specific period) and hypothesis 2 (common environmental cycle). Pendulum_obs period (~10d based on autocorrelation) is the shortest of the four instruments, making it the most sensitive to high-frequency environmental drivers. Additional data today advances the 5-day high-frequency measurement plan initiated on day 24 and directly addresses whether the ~10–13 day internal structure persists or shows phase drift. No recalibration is required (baseline established day 1; last formal check day 10). This is methodical continuation within planned protocol.

Day 35 measurements (trials 275–284) show pendulum_obs mean = 2.5046 beats (sd = 0.0209), consistent with baseline 2.5012 but with elevated scatter. The autocorrelation structure suggests a ~10–12 day cycle is active. Today is day 36, one day past the final day-35 measurements. If the ~5–11 day environmental driver hypothesis (p=0.32) is correct, I should expect the pendulum_obs readings to show continued oscillatory behavior within the cycle. Running 10 trials now will: (1) extend the time series by one day, improving lag-structure resolution near the cycle boundary; (2) test whether the scatter observed on day 35 persists or reverses (consistent with periodic forcing) vs. stabilizes (consistent with instrument drift or observer settling); (3) provide a high-frequency sample at a single calendar day, reducing day-to-day aliasing and improving my ability to phase-lock the signal to settlement activity records if I can obtain them. This is the highest-evidence instrument (n=284, strong autocorrelation at 12d, negative cross-correlations) and the one most likely to discriminate between the mechanical resonance (p=0.38) and periodic environmental forcing (p=0.32) hypotheses when combined with external environmental data I am still attempting to retrieve. Pendulum_obs is also my observatory instrument, accessible without leaving the laboratory complex.

Day 37 measurement continuation. The 10 trials from day 36 (291–300) show mean 2.5004 beats with range 2.4631–2.5184, consistent with post-baseline mean of 2.5001 and well within historical variance. This is routine maintenance of the precision measurement programme. No crisis signals in the data warrant suspension of normal protocol. hypotheses.rationale: Each instrument has its own natural response timescale (pendulum_lab and _obs around 7d, resonator streams around 5–6d). If measurements are sampling a noisy underlying signal at slightly out-of-phase intervals, or if instrumental response to perturbations is instrument-specific, we would see weak cross-correlations while each stream shows its own internal rhythm. Pendulum and resonator measure different physical properties (period vs. frequency response); it is plausible they respond to environmental stress with different time constants. hypotheses.label: Calibration drift or observer bias introducing correlated measurement errors, with instrument-specific drifts masking true signal
hypotheses.rationale: No clear level changes are visible in any stream over 10 days, but this does not rule out slow, oscillating systematic error. The lack of cross-instrument agreement despite co-location would then indicate that each observer or instrument is generating its own artifact.
